sounds.intro: Hawaiian has only eight consonants (h, k, l, m, n, p, w and the ʻokina) and five vowels. Every vowel is said. The ʻokina (ʻ) is a short stop in the voice, like the break in "uh-oh". The kahakō (ā) is a bar over a long vowel. Both change the meaning.
rows: a catch in the voice, like the break in "uh-oh"
the same vowel, held about twice as long
"w" after o or u, "v" or "w" after a or e
ai / ae / ao / au / ei / eu / oi / ou
a pair of vowels said together, each sound still clear
notes: Hawaiian has no "s". The stress usually falls on the second-last syllable, and on long vowels. Aloha has stress on "lo".
There is no verb "to be". A sentence like "He haumāna au" is "A student I", meaning "I am a student".

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Hawaiian has no he / she difference: "ia" means both. It has a dual "we" (two people) and a plural "we" (three or more), and each comes in two kinds: "kāua / kākou" includes the listener, "māua / mākou" excludes the listener.

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: Nouns do not change. Use "ka" or "ke" (the) for one, and "nā" (the) for many: ka puke (the book), nā puke (the books). Use "he mau" before a noun for "some": he mau puke.

grammar.title: To be: he, ʻo, aia
text: Hawaiian has no verb "to be". Use "he" before a noun (he kumu au, a teacher I), "ʻo" for a name or identity, and "aia" for places (aia au ma ka hale). An adjective can stand first.

grammar.title: Having: he ... koʻu
text: To say "I have", Hawaiian says "a ... mine": he kaʻa koʻu (a car mine). Use "koʻu" for things you own that you do not control (o-class) and "kaʻu" for things you can give away or do (a-class).

grammar.title: Present tense
text: Verbs do not change for person. Put "ke" before the verb and "nei" after it for now: ke ʻai nei au (I am eating). Without "ke ... nei", it is simply "I eat".
ex: ke ʻai nei au i ka berena

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The verb comes first. The order is verb, subject, object: "heluhelu au i ka puke" (read I the book). "I" marks the object.

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: Raise your voice at the end, or add "anei" after the first word: "Makemake anei ʻoe?" (Do you want?). To answer, repeat the verb or say "ʻae" (yes) or "ʻaʻole" (no).

grammar.title: Question words
text: Question words usually come at the start or in the place of the answer.
ex: i ka manawa hea ka haʻawina?

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: There are two kinds of "my": "koʻu" (things you have, can't choose, like family and body) and "kaʻu" (things you choose or do, like a pencil or a plan). Your: kou / kāu. His, her: kona / kāna. Our: ko mākou / kā mākou.

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: Hawaiian shows respect with "ʻoukou" (you, plural) for one person, and with "e ʻoluʻolu" (please). There is no formal verb form.

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Verbs do not change. Past: put "ua" before the verb (ua ʻai au, I ate). Future: put "e" before the verb and "ana" after (e ʻai ana au, I will eat).

grammar.title: Commands
text: Put "e" before the verb: e hele mai (come). To forbid, use "mai" before the verb: mai hele (do not go).
